item.stem: Two fats have fatty acid chains of similar lengths. Fat X contains more unsaturated fatty acids and is liquid at room temperature, while fat Y contains more saturated fatty acids and is solid. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?

choices.choice_text: Unsaturated fatty acids in fat X contain only single carbon–carbon bonds, which introduce kinks.
choices.rationale: Saturation reversal: saturated, not unsaturated, fatty acids contain only single carbon–carbon bonds. The kinks associated with unsaturation result from double bonds. Fix: Match saturated with single bonds and unsaturated with at least one double bond.

choices.choice_text: Double bonds straighten fat X’s fatty acid chains, allowing tighter packing.
choices.rationale: Packing reversal: the double bonds associated with unsaturation introduce kinks rather than straighten the chains. Reduced tight packing helps explain why fat X is liquid. Fix: Trace the relationship from double bonds to kinks to reduced packing.

choices.choice_text: Double bonds make fat X’s fatty acid chains hydrophilic, causing it to be liquid.
choices.rationale: Polarity confusion: carbon–carbon double bonds do not make fatty acid chains hydrophilic; the chains remain largely nonpolar. The relevant difference is chain packing, not attraction to water. Fix: Distinguish a fatty acid chain’s saturation from its polarity.

choices.choice_text: Double bonds introduce kinks in fat X’s fatty acid chains, preventing tight packing.
choices.rationale: Unsaturated fatty acids contain carbon–carbon double bonds that introduce kinks. These kinks reduce tight packing, making fat X more likely to be liquid at room temperature.

item.stem: A bakery tests a modified canola oil in which some carbon–carbon double bonds in the fatty acid chains have been converted to single bonds. The chain lengths remain unchanged. Which prediction best connects this modification to the oil’s texture at room temperature?

choices.choice_text: The oil tends to become firmer because fewer kinks allow the fatty acid chains to pack more tightly.
choices.rationale: Converting double bonds to single bonds increases saturation and reduces the kinks associated with unsaturation. Straighter chains pack more tightly, favoring a firmer texture at room temperature.

choices.choice_text: The oil tends to become firmer because the chains become more unsaturated, and unsaturated chains contain only single carbon–carbon bonds.
choices.rationale: Saturation reversal: chains with only single carbon–carbon bonds are saturated, whereas unsaturated chains have at least one double bond. This modification increases saturation rather than unsaturation. Fix: Identify whether the modification increases or decreases the number of double bonds.

choices.choice_text: The oil tends to become softer because removing double bonds introduces kinks that prevent tight packing.
choices.rationale: Packing reversal: removing the double bonds associated with kinks reduces bending rather than adding it. The resulting chains can pack more tightly, favoring firmness rather than softness. Fix: Follow the sequence from fewer double bonds to fewer kinks to tighter packing.

choices.choice_text: The oil tends to become firmer because converting double bonds to single bonds changes the chains from hydrophilic to hydrophobic.
choices.rationale: Polarity confusion: both saturated and unsaturated fatty acid chains are largely nonpolar. The texture change follows altered chain packing, not a switch from attraction to water to avoidance of water. Fix: Check whether the proposed explanation concerns chain shape or attraction to water.

item.stem: A cosmetics manufacturer needs a fat that flows easily at room temperature for use in a skin lotion. The available fats have fatty acid chains of comparable lengths but differ in saturation. Which recommendation best explains how to obtain the desired consistency?

choices.choice_text: Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because these chains have only single carbon–carbon bonds, which create bends.
choices.rationale: Saturation reversal: chains with only single carbon–carbon bonds are saturated, whereas unsaturated chains contain double bonds. The bends associated with unsaturation arise from double bonds, not single bonds. Fix: Check which bond type defines each saturation category before predicting texture.

choices.choice_text: Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because double bonds straighten the chains and promote close packing.
choices.rationale: Packing reversal: double bonds associated with unsaturation produce bends rather than straighter chains. Close packing would favor a firmer fat, not the flowing consistency needed here. Fix: Link chain bending to packing before deciding whether a fat will flow.

choices.choice_text: Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because double bonds bend the chains and reduce tight packing.
choices.rationale: Kinks produced by carbon–carbon double bonds keep unsaturated fatty acid chains from packing closely together. A fat with more of these chains is therefore more likely to remain liquid at room temperature.

choices.choice_text: Select a fat rich in unsaturated fatty acids because double bonds make the chains hydrophilic and therefore liquid.
choices.rationale: Polarity confusion: adding carbon–carbon double bonds does not make fatty acid chains hydrophilic; they remain largely nonpolar. Their effect on consistency comes from altered packing, not increased attraction to water. Fix: Separate changes in chain shape from changes in attraction to water.

item.stem: An agricultural laboratory examines oils extracted from sunflower seeds grown in two fields. The northern field’s oil contains a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids than the southern field’s oil, while fatty acid chain lengths are similar. Which prediction about the northern field’s oil at room temperature is best supported by its fatty acid structure?

choices.choice_text: It should be more likely to remain liquid because unsaturated fatty acids have only single carbon–carbon bonds that create kinks.
choices.rationale: Saturation reversal: this explanation assigns single bonds to unsaturated fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids have only single carbon–carbon bonds; the kinks associated with unsaturation arise from double bonds. Fix: Identify whether each fatty acid has only single bonds or includes double bonds.

choices.choice_text: It should be more likely to become solid because double bonds straighten fatty acid chains and promote tight packing.
choices.rationale: Packing reversal: this prediction treats double bonds as chain-straightening features. The kinks associated with unsaturation reduce tight packing rather than promote it. Fix: Link increased unsaturation to chain shape, then use that shape to predict packing.

choices.choice_text: It should be more likely to remain liquid because double bonds make fatty acid chains hydrophilic.
choices.rationale: Polarity confusion: this explanation mistakes unsaturation for increased attraction to water. Fatty acid chains remain largely nonpolar; their packing explains the predicted consistency difference. Fix: Separate the question of chain polarity from the question of chain packing.

choices.choice_text: It should be more likely to remain liquid because double bonds create kinks that reduce tight packing of fatty acid chains.
choices.rationale: A higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids means more chains with carbon–carbon double bonds and associated kinks. These chains pack less tightly, favoring a liquid consistency at room temperature.

item.stem:
A student compares three fat samples whose fatty acid chains have the same length but different numbers of carbon–carbon double bonds. The student records the following results.

Sample | Double bonds per fatty acid chain | Melting temperature (°C)
X | 0 | 60
Y | 1 | 15
Z | 2 | −5

Which statement best describes the relationship in the data and explains it using fatty acid structure?

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with higher melting temperatures because unsaturated fatty acid chains are straighter and pack more closely.
choices.rationale: Reversed-trend trap: The recorded melting temperatures decrease, rather than increase, with more double bonds. Unsaturated chains have kinks, rather than being straighter. Fix: Track melting temperature from zero to two double bonds before describing the trend.

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with lower melting temperatures because kinks in unsaturated fatty acid chains interfere with close packing.
choices.rationale: Melting temperature decreases from 60°C to −5°C as the number of double bonds increases. Double bonds introduce kinks that prevent close packing, helping explain why more unsaturated fats remain liquid at lower temperatures.

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with lower melting temperatures because double bonds make the fats hydrophilic.
choices.rationale: Polarity-confusion trap: The trend is described accurately, but unsaturation does not make these fats hydrophilic. Fats remain generally nonpolar; chain kinks explain the melting-temperature pattern. Fix: Distinguish changes in chain shape from changes in attraction to water.

choices.choice_text: More double bonds are associated with lower melting temperatures because adding double bonds makes the fatty acid chains more saturated.
choices.rationale: Saturation-definition trap: The trend is described accurately, but adding double bonds increases unsaturation, not saturation. Saturated fatty acid chains contain only single carbon–carbon bonds. Fix: Check for carbon–carbon double bonds before classifying a fatty acid as saturated.

item.stem:
A bakery tests three fat blends to find one that stays mostly liquid at 20°C. The fatty acid chains are equal in length across the blends. Measurements at 20°C give these results:

Blend | Average carbon–carbon double bonds per fatty acid chain | Percentage of fat that is liquid
P | 0 | 0%
Q | 1 | 60%
R | 2 | 100%

Which statement accurately describes the pattern and connects it to fatty acid structure?

choices.choice_text: As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage increases because kinked fatty acid chains cannot pack as closely.
choices.rationale: The liquid percentage rises from 0% to 100% as the average double-bond count increases. Double bonds introduce chain kinks that disrupt close packing, helping more unsaturated fats remain liquid at the test temperature.

choices.choice_text: As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage decreases because unsaturated fatty acid chains are straight and pack tightly.
choices.rationale: Reversed-trend trap: The liquid percentage increases, not decreases, with double-bond count. Unsaturated chains contain kinks rather than being straight. Fix: Follow the liquid percentages as double-bond count rises before stating the relationship.

choices.choice_text: As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage increases because the fats become hydrophilic.
choices.rationale: Polarity-confusion trap: This identifies the observed increase but incorrectly attributes it to attraction to water. Unsaturation changes chain shape without making these generally nonpolar fats hydrophilic. Fix: Separate changes in chain shape from changes in water attraction.

choices.choice_text: As double bonds become more numerous, the liquid percentage increases because the fatty acid chains become more saturated.
choices.rationale: Saturation-definition trap: The liquid-percentage pattern is accurate, but more double bonds mean greater unsaturation. Saturated fatty acid chains have only single carbon–carbon bonds. Fix: Count carbon–carbon double bonds before deciding whether saturation increases.

item.stem:
A skin-care company is selecting a fat blend for a lotion stored at cool temperatures. All fatty acid chains in the blends have the same length, and each unsaturated chain contains one carbon–carbon double bond. The company obtains these measurements:

Blend | Saturated fatty acid chains (%) | Melting temperature (°C)
Rose | 20 | 5
Fern | 50 | 18
Moss | 80 | 32

Which statement correctly summarizes the measured relationship and connects it to fatty acid structure?

choices.choice_text: Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at lower temperatures because saturated chains have more kinks.
choices.rationale: Reversed-trend trap: The measurements show increasing, not decreasing, melting temperatures as the saturated proportion rises. The structural explanation also reverses the relationship: double bonds in unsaturated chains introduce kinks. Fix: Follow the temperature values as the saturated percentage increases, then check which chains contain kinks.

choices.choice_text: Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at higher temperatures because saturation makes fats hydrophilic.
choices.rationale: Polarity-confusion trap: The temperature pattern is described correctly, but saturation does not make fats hydrophilic. Differences in chain shape and packing, rather than attraction to water, explain this pattern. Fix: Separate a change in chain packing from a change in water attraction.

choices.choice_text: Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at higher temperatures because saturated chains contain more carbon–carbon double bonds.
choices.rationale: Saturation-definition trap: The measured trend is accurate, but the definition of saturation is reversed. Saturated fatty acid chains have only single carbon–carbon bonds; double bonds indicate unsaturation. Fix: Identify the carbon–carbon bond types before deciding whether a chain is saturated.

choices.choice_text: Blends with a greater percentage of saturated chains melt at higher temperatures because straighter chains can pack more closely.
choices.rationale: Melting temperature rises from 5°C to 32°C as the saturated proportion increases from 20% to 80%. Saturated chains lack the double-bond kinks of unsaturated chains, allowing closer packing that helps explain the higher melting temperatures.

item.stem:
An animal-feed supplier needs a fat that remains solid in a cool warehouse. Three candidate fats have equal-length fatty acid chains but differ in their degree of unsaturation. Testing produces the following measurements:

Fat | Average carbon–carbon double bonds per fatty acid chain | Melting temperature (°C)
Cedar | 3 | −12
Maple | 2 | 8
Pine | 0 | 48

As the average number of double bonds decreases, which statement describes the measured trend and explains its structural basis?

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature falls because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds have more kinks and pack less closely.
choices.rationale: Reversed-trend trap: The measurements show rising melting temperatures as double bonds decrease, not falling temperatures. Removing double bonds also reduces the kinks associated with unsaturation rather than adding them. Fix: Follow the rows from three double bonds to zero and compare their melting temperatures.

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds make the fats hydrophilic.
choices.rationale: Polarity-confusion trap: This identifies the temperature trend but incorrectly attributes it to attraction to water. These fats remain generally hydrophobic; differences in chain shape and packing explain the pattern. Fix: Separate the number of chain kinks from whether a fat interacts favorably with water.

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer double bonds are more unsaturated.
choices.rationale: Saturation-definition trap: This matches the measured temperature trend but reverses the meaning of unsaturation. Fewer carbon–carbon double bonds indicate less unsaturation, and chains with none are saturated. Fix: Count carbon–carbon double bonds before comparing the degree of unsaturation.

choices.choice_text: Melting temperature rises because fatty acid chains with fewer kinks can pack together more closely.
choices.rationale: Moving from three double bonds to zero, the measured melting temperature rises from −12°C to 48°C. Fewer double bonds mean fewer chain kinks, allowing closer packing and helping explain the higher melting temperature.

Describing a data trend and the relationship between variables is 4.B. It applies a single concept to the data, so it is Medium.

choices.choice_text: It will tend to be less liquid and will remain suitable for energy storage.
choices.rationale: Converting double bonds to single bonds increases saturation, reducing kinks and allowing fatty acid chains to pack more closely. This favors a less liquid consistency at room temperature without eliminating the energy-storage function of fats.

item.stem: In a certain plant, an enzyme inserts carbon–carbon double bonds into the fatty acid tails of membrane phospholipids. A mutant plant lacks this enzyme, so its phospholipids contain only saturated fatty acid tails. Wild-type and mutant plants are moved from 25°C to 5°C. Which prediction about the mutant's cell membranes at 5°C, compared with wild-type membranes, is best supported?

choices.choice_text: The mutant's membranes will be more fluid, because straight saturated tails slide past one another more easily than kinked tails.
choices.rationale: This reverses the effect of kinks: students picture straight tails as slippery. In fact, straight saturated tails pack tightly and resist movement, while kinks from double bonds create spacing that increases fluidity. Fix: Ask whether each tail shape lets neighboring tails pack closely or keeps them apart.

choices.choice_text: The mutant's phospholipids will fail to form a bilayer, because saturated tails become polar and attract water.
choices.rationale: This confuses saturation with polarity. Removing double bonds changes tail shape and packing, not charge; saturated hydrocarbon tails remain nonpolar and hydrophobic, so the bilayer still forms. Fix: Check whether a change alters polarity or only shape before predicting effects on bilayer formation.

choices.choice_text: The mutant's membranes will be less fluid, because straight saturated tails pack tightly together, which likely restricts the movement and function of membrane proteins.
choices.rationale: Double bonds create kinks that keep fatty acid tails from packing closely, so unsaturated lipids stay more fluid in the cold. Without kinks, saturated tails pack tightly and the membrane stiffens at low temperature, which likely impairs proteins that must move within or change shape in the bilayer.

choices.choice_text: The mutant's membranes will be unchanged, because only stored fats, not membrane phospholipids, contain fatty acid tails.
choices.rationale: This misidentifies phospholipid structure: phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate-containing head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails. The stem states the enzyme acts on phospholipid tails, so membranes are directly affected. Fix: List the parts of each lipid type and check which parts the described change affects.

choices.rationale: Additional carbon–carbon double bonds introduce kinks that limit tight packing, making the fats more liquid at the comparison temperature. This structural change neither makes the fats water-soluble nor changes their role as energy reserves.

choices.choice_text: The reserves become less liquid but remain hydrophobic fats that store energy.
choices.rationale: Reversed packing effect: This prediction assumes that greater unsaturation allows fatty acid chains to pack more closely. Double-bond kinks interfere with close packing, favoring increased rather than decreased liquidity. Fix: Sketch straight and kinked chains, then compare how closely they can pack.

choices.choice_text: The reserves become more liquid and dissolve in water, losing their energy-storage role.
choices.rationale: Liquid–soluble confusion: This prediction treats becoming liquid as becoming water-soluble. Unsaturated fats remain hydrophobic and can still function as energy reserves. Fix: Check whether the change affects packing, water solubility, or both.

choices.choice_text: The reserves become more liquid and assemble into phospholipid bilayers, replacing their energy-storage role.
choices.rationale: Lipid-class interchangeability: This prediction incorrectly turns a change within stored fats into a change of lipid class. Increasing unsaturation does not create phospholipids or transfer their bilayer-forming function to fats. Fix: Name the lipid class before predicting whether its biological role changes.
